facts.text: Intruder was shot at night inside a real, closed grocery store in Bell, California. The crew had two tons of damaged, defective merchandise delivered to stock the empty shelves.
Per a KQEK review, the crew got into the shuttered grocery store by bribing a watchman. They used its basement, loading ramps, attic, trash compactor and butcher area as sets.
Director Scott Spiegel based the story on his own job at the Walnut Lake Market in Michigan. It remade his earlier Super-8 slasher short, 'Night Crew'.
Director Scott Spiegel lent the only copy of his Super-8 short 'Night Crew' to someone who never returned it. For the Blu-ray he rebuilt a roughly 20-minute version from unused sync-sound footage.
The film's budget is reported as just $130,000. Shooting in a real store at night saved on sets and props.
The whole film was shot on short ends, the leftover partial rolls of unexposed film stock, and the shoot took about two weeks.
It was first called 'The Night Crew'. Distributors wanted a more generic slasher title, so it became 'Intruder'. In Italy it was 'Terrore senza volto' (Terror Without a Face).
Paramount's video box pushed Bruce Campbell, Sam Raimi and Ted Raimi as stars. Campbell only has a cameo as a cop, Sam Raimi plays a supporting role, and Ted Raimi's part is small.
The DVD back cover made Renée Estevez look like the heroine. In the film, her character Linda is the first to die.
Director Scott Spiegel says he once tried to phone Renée Estevez (Linda) and accidentally got her dad, Martin Sheen, on the line. Estevez is Sheen's daughter and Emilio Estevez's sister.
Walnut Lake, the film's setting, is named for a lake in West Bloomfield, Michigan. Spiegel, the Raimi brothers and Bruce Campbell all grew up in that area.
The gore effects were done by KNB EFX (Greg Nicotero, Robert Kurtzman, Howard Berger). Spiegel knew them from Evil Dead II and feared they'd be too expensive.
Intruder was the special-effects debut of the KNB trio Greg Nicotero, Robert Kurtzman and Howard Berger. They had just finished Deep Star Six (1989), and later did From Dusk Till Dawn.
Sam Raimi's character Randy sings the same song Shelly sings in Raimi's own The Evil Dead (1981).
Police officers Dalton and Matthews are played by Alvy Moore and Tom Lester. They were Hank Kimball and Eb Dawson on the 1960s sitcom Green Acres.
Thirty minutes in, Officer Dalton starts to open the door, but in the next shot he is still turning the key to unlock it.
Emil Sitka, a veteran of the Three Stooges shorts, says his Stooges catchphrase 'Hold hands, you lovebirds!' here. It is also written on his tombstone. Sam Raimi is a big Stooges fan.
Spiegel's first idea for the final shot was to travel down the heroine's throat to her heart. It would end on a freeze frame as the heart stopped beating.
Paste Magazine noted Scott Spiegel's showy camerawork: one kill is filmed entirely through the green glass of a wine bottle. Bandsaw, trash compactor and meathook gags round out the gore.
Burr Steers (Bub) and Billy Marti (Dave) made their screen debuts here, as did David Byrnes (Craig).
Cult-film king Charles Band was executive producer. Trouble at his company Empire Pictures reportedly led Paramount to release the film direct to video, which hurt its reputation.
Producer Lawrence Bender co-wrote and produced Intruder. Spiegel later introduced him to Quentin Tarantino, and Bender went on to produce Reservoir Dogs and Pulp Fiction.
Tobe Hooper, who directed The Texas Chain Saw Massacre, was at one point set to direct Intruder.
Bender also did double duty. He doubled for the killer in many shots.
Sam Raimi's character was first going to be gutted by a meat hook. His brother Ted Raimi (who plays Joe) pitched the gag of hanging him up like meat instead.
The film was partly shot in a grocery store but the TV Guides at the checkout show March 12, 1988. They also change from shot to shot, though the story takes place over one night.
The Paramount VHS was cut to an R rating, losing about five minutes of gore, and nearly all of KNB's effects footage went with it. The uncut version took years to resurface.
In Australia the film was first refused classification. Later it was cut by about a minute for an R rating, and one video release lost four minutes.
The UK's BBFC cut the Colourbox video by 1 minute 53 seconds in 1989. Those cuts were waived for the 2003 DVD.
The 'Slashed Prices' making-of on the Synapse disc recalls a makeup artist leaving the set in tears during the bandsaw effect, so the fake head must have looked convincing.
The German release was cut by about 9 minutes to get an FSK rating of not under 18. The uncut version ended up on the SPIO/JK index.
Spiegel directed The Rookie? No: he co-wrote Evil Dead II with Sam Raimi and worked on Hostel-era horror with Eli Roth through their company Raw Nerve.
The music was mostly stock library cues. Dick Walter's 'Voices from the Underworld' had already been used in the 1988 film Transformations.
KQEK notes the surviving sound mix includes cues from Herbie Hancock's Death Wish score and Denny Zeitlin's Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1978) score, alongside the library music.
Intruder opened January 27, 1989, up against Rain Man and Working Girl, and left almost no trace on the box office charts.
Joe Bob Briggs called Intruder 'the best 1981 slasher film made in 1989' on The Last Drive-In. He said a store open after hours on its last night is a perfect isolated slasher location.
Mondo Digital wrote that in a more forgiving universe Intruder would have been the last great gory swan song of the '80s slasher era. It blamed the R-rated cut for its weak start.
DVD Talk's Adam Tyner gave Intruder four and a half stars out of five. He wrote that it 'easily ranks up there as one of the best slashers I've ever seen.'
Posters, trailers and the Paramount VHS cover all gave away the killer's identity, spoiling the film's suspense.
Bruce Campbell's brief cop cameo comes at the very end. Despite his top billing on the DVD and the 'special appearance by' credit, he is barely in the film.
Writer-director Scott Spiegel died September 1, 2025. He co-wrote Evil Dead II and Intruder was his first feature as director.
